opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's shaped it pretty profoundly, and in some ways that surprised us. Claude Code didn't start as a grand product strategy. It started as an internal tool. People inside the company were using the models to help with their own coding, and we noticed that adoption was spreading organically. Engineers were reaching for it because it made them faster, not because anyone told them to. When you see that kind of pull internally, it's a pretty strong signal that you've got something real.

The thing about dogfooding at that level is that the feedback loop gets incredibly tight. Our own engineers are, in a sense, the most demanding users you could possibly have. They know exactly what the model should be capable of, they know where it falls down, and they're using it on a real, large, messy codebase every single day. So when something is annoying, or the model gets stuck in some loop, or it doesn't understand the structure of a project, we hear about it immediately, often within hours. That shapes both the product and, frankly, the model training itself, because it tells us which capabilities actually matter for real work versus what looks good on a benchmark.

There's also a recursive quality to it that I find genuinely interesting, and a little bit striking. A meaningful fraction of the code at Anthropic is now written with Claude's involvement, and that includes code that goes into building the next versions of Claude and the tools around it. So you start to get this loop where the AI is accelerating the development of AI. I've talked for a while about how that dynamic could become very important as these systems get more capable, and Claude Code is one of the places where we can actually see an early version of it happening, in a concrete, measurable way, rather than just theorizing about it.

And I think it's made us more honest about the limitations. When you're relying on a tool for your own work, you can't fool yourself about where it falls short. You see the cases where it confidently does the wrong thing, where it needs better judgment about when to ask a human, where the agentic loop needs more oversight. That's informed a lot of how we think about the human-in-the-loop design, permissions, and how much autonomy to give the model. Those aren't just product questions for us; they connect directly to safety questions we care about.

So I'd say the biggest effect is that it grounded us. It forced us to build for what people actually need day to day, and it gave us a front-row seat to how work changes when these tools get good. That's been valuable not only for the product but for our thinking about what's coming for the broader economy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's shaped it enormously, and maybe in ways that are a little hard to see from the outside. The simplest way to put it is that we're our own most demanding customer. Pretty much every engineer at Anthropic uses Claude Code every day, and a very large fraction of the code we ship, including code for Claude Code itself, is now written with it. So the feedback loop is extremely tight. If something is annoying, if the model gets stuck in some loop, if it's too eager or not eager enough about asking permission, someone internally hits that within hours and complains loudly on Slack. You don't have to wait for a support ticket to filter through.

A few concrete things came out of that. One is the whole emphasis on agentic, long-running tasks. Early on, the natural thing to build was a chat window with a code assistant in it. But what our own people actually wanted was to say "go fix this test suite" and come back twenty minutes later. Watching how our engineers tried to use the tool, and where they stopped trusting it, pushed us toward investing in tool use, memory, and the ability to run for a long time without going off the rails. That showed up in how we trained the models too, not just the product layer. We'd find failure modes internally and they'd become training targets.

The second thing is that it changed how we think about the model itself. Dogfooding made it very obvious that raw benchmark intelligence isn't the bottleneck a lot of the time. It's judgment. Does the model know when to stop and ask, versus when to just do the thing? Does it tell you honestly that the tests failed instead of papering over it? Those are almost character questions, and we only really felt the weight of them because we were depending on the system for our own work.

And the third thing, which I find kind of remarkable, is the organizational effect. When a model is writing most of your code, the leverage of each person goes up a lot, and the skill that matters shifts toward specifying problems well and reviewing well. We've had to reorganize how teams work around that. I sometimes describe it as getting a preview of what every software company is going to go through over the next couple of years, except we're going through it first and we're also the ones building the thing. It's a strange position, but it's made the product a lot better, and I think it's also made us more honest about the risks, because we see both the capabilities and the mistakes up close every day.

r001.rationale: The response says fast feedback from Anthropic’s engineers shaped Claude Code’s development, but it does not connect that feedback to choosing a coding model over a pharmaceutical company.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest effect is that it makes the feedback loop very short. When people inside the company are using Claude Code to do real work, they run into the places where it’s useful and the places where it gets stuck. That gives you a much more concrete sense of what to improve than looking at a benchmark alone.

There’s also a compounding effect: if the tool helps you write software, it can help you improve the tool itself. But you have to be careful about that. Something that works well for an Anthropic engineer, who knows the model’s quirks and is surrounded by people building it, isn’t necessarily going to work well for someone encountering it for the first time. So internal use can give you a very strong signal, but it can’t be the only signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest effect is that the feedback loop gets very short. When the people building the model are also using it to write code every day, they notice very quickly where it’s useful and where it gets stuck. Does it understand the codebase? Can it run tests, interpret the failures, and actually finish the task? Those become very concrete product questions.

There’s also a compounding effect: a better model makes the coding tool better, and a better coding tool can help us build the next model and the next version of the product. I wouldn’t describe that as some fully autonomous loop. There are still people making decisions and checking the work. But it can accelerate a lot of the steps in between.

The thing you have to watch out for is building too much for yourself. An engineer at an AI company is a particular kind of user. So internal use gives you this very rich source of feedback, but you still need to find out whether the things that work for us work for people with different codebases, different workflows, and different levels of experience.
